name: Aflatoxicosis

agents.name: Aflatoxin B1
agents.notes: The most toxic and most common of the aflatoxins, produced by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus. Aflatoxin B1 is a potent hepatotoxin and the most potent natural carcinogen known. It is activated by hepatic cytochrome P450 to an epoxide that binds DNA and protein, causing hepatocellular necrosis and mutations.

agents.name: Aspergillus flavus
agents.notes: A ubiquitous mould that colonises stored grains, oilseeds and nuts. Growth and toxin production are favoured by warm temperatures (25-33 degrees Celsius), high humidity and insect or mechanical damage to the seed coat. Aflatoxin production is not visible — the mould may be present without toxin, and toxin may be present in feed that looks normal.
agents.reservoir: Contaminated stored grain, groundnuts, cottonseed, maize and their by-products

agents.name: Aspergillus parasiticus
agents.notes: A closely related species that produces both the B and G series of aflatoxins. It is less common than A. flavus but is a significant source of contamination in groundnuts in particular.

hosts.notes: All animals are susceptible, but ruminants are generally more resistant to acute aflatoxicosis than pigs and poultry. Dairy cattle are a special concern because they convert aflatoxin B1 to aflatoxin M1, which is excreted in milk and is a regulated human food contaminant.

notifiable.note: Aflatoxin is a regulated food and feed contaminant rather than a notifiable animal disease. Human exposure is a major public health issue across sub-Saharan Africa, where aflatoxin contamination of staple maize and groundnuts is widespread and contributes to liver cancer and childhood stunting.

distribution: Endemic in tropical and subtropical regions with warm, humid climates. Sub-Saharan Africa has among the highest dietary aflatoxin exposure levels in the world. In southern Africa, contamination of maize, groundnuts and sorghum is a recurring problem, particularly in years with a wet growing season and poor storage conditions.

aetiology.summary: Aflatoxicosis is caused by ingestion of feed contaminated with aflatoxins produced by Aspergillus moulds growing on poorly stored grain and oilseeds. The toxin is heat-stable and survives normal feed processing, so the only reliable control is preventing mould growth and rejecting contaminated batches.
determinants: Presence of aflatoxin-producing Aspergillus on the feed
Warm, humid storage conditions that allow mould growth and toxin production
Insect or mechanical damage to grain, which provides entry points for the fungus
Prolonged storage of grain at high moisture content
The dose and duration of exposure — chronic low-level exposure is more common than acute poisoning
risk_factors: Feeding stored maize, groundnuts or cottonseed that has been poorly dried or stored
Warm, humid climates and rainy harvests
Damaged or mouldy grain, particularly that which has been damp or insect-infested
Feeding dairy cows contaminated concentrate — the milk residue risk is the critical issue
Feeding pigs and poultry on contaminated rations, as they are the most susceptible species
Poor storage in sacks on the floor, without ventilation or moisture control
aetiology.epidemiology: Aflatoxicosis is a feed-borne problem that affects groups of animals receiving the same ration. Acute outbreaks occur when a highly contaminated batch enters the feed chain. Chronic low-level exposure is far more common and produces subclinical effects — reduced growth, immunosuppression and reduced fertility — which are easy to overlook. In dairy cattle, the economic issue is often the milk residue rather than the cow's health.

pathophysiology.summary: Aflatoxin B1 is absorbed from the gut and transported to the liver, where cytochrome P450 converts it to a reactive epoxide. The epoxide binds covalently to DNA and proteins, causing hepatocellular necrosis, inhibition of protein synthesis and, with chronic exposure, DNA mutations that initiate liver tumours. The same mechanism explains the immunosuppression and the reduced growth.

cascade.title: Ingestion and hepatic uptake
cascade.detail: Aflatoxin B1 is absorbed from the small intestine and transported to the liver via the portal circulation, where it is concentrated in hepatocytes.

cascade.title: Metabolic activation
cascade.detail: Cytochrome P450 enzymes convert aflatoxin B1 to a highly reactive 8,9-epoxide, which is the toxic and carcinogenic metabolite. The balance between activation and detoxification determines species susceptibility.

cascade.title: DNA and protein adduct formation
cascade.detail: The epoxide binds covalently to guanine residues in DNA and to lysine residues in proteins. DNA adducts cause mutations, particularly in the p53 tumour suppressor gene, and protein adducts impair enzyme function and cause cellular injury.

cascade.title: Hepatocellular necrosis and impaired protein synthesis
cascade.detail: Acute high-dose exposure produces centrilobular hepatic necrosis with jaundice and haemorrhage. Chronic exposure inhibits protein synthesis, reducing growth, milk production and immune function.

cascade.title: Immunosuppression, carcinogenesis and milk residues
cascade.detail: Chronic exposure suppresses cell-mediated immunity, increasing susceptibility to infectious disease. In the long term, DNA damage leads to hepatocellular carcinoma. In dairy cattle, aflatoxin B1 is converted to aflatoxin M1 and excreted in milk, creating a human food safety issue even when the cow shows no clinical signs.

lesions: Enlarged, pale, yellow-brown liver with centrilobular necrosis
Gall bladder distension with thickened bile
Subcutaneous and visceral haemorrhages from impaired clotting factor synthesis
Jaundice and generalised oedema in acute cases
Hepatic fibrosis and, in chronic cases, nodular regeneration and tumours
Atrophy of the thymus and lymphoid tissues in chronic exposure
clinical_signs: Reduced feed intake and growth rate
Weight loss and poor feed conversion
Jaundice and pale mucous membranes in acute cases
Reduced milk yield in dairy cattle
Increased susceptibility to infectious disease from immunosuppression
In pigs: reduced growth, and in severe cases, abortion
In poultry: reduced growth, poor feathering and increased mortality
In acute outbreaks: sudden death in young animals

antemortem: Feed analysis for total aflatoxin concentration — the most direct approach
Serum liver enzyme activity, particularly AST and GGT, which reflects hepatocellular damage
Serum bile acids or bilirubin in cases with jaundice
Feeding history and a comparison with unaffected groups on a different ration
postmortem: Examine the liver for pallor, enlargement and necrosis
Submit liver tissue for histopathology and feed samples for toxin analysis
laboratory: Feed analysis by HPLC, ELISA or lateral flow tests for aflatoxin
Liver histopathology showing centrilobular necrosis and bile duct proliferation
Detection of aflatoxin M1 in milk, which is a regulatory test in many countries
Aflatoxin-DNA or albumin adduct measurement in research and human biomonitoring
differentials: Other mycotoxins — fumonisin, ochratoxin, deoxynivalenol, which produce different syndromes
Pyrrolizidine alkaloid poisoning from plants such as ragwort and Crotalaria — similar hepatic damage
Copper poisoning — jaundice and hepatic necrosis with a different exposure history
Photosensitisation from liver damage, which can be a consequence of aflatoxicosis rather than an alternative

prevention: Dry grain to below the safe moisture level before storage and keep it dry
Store feed in cool, dry, well-ventilated conditions and prevent insect damage
Test incoming feed batches for aflatoxin, particularly maize, groundnuts and cottonseed
Buy feed from suppliers with a documented mycotoxin testing programme
Use a mould inhibitor or organic acid preservative in high-risk feeds
Rotate feed stocks and avoid prolonged storage in humid conditions
control.vaccination: Not applicable — no vaccine exists for mycotoxicosis. A vaccine for human aflatoxin exposure is in development but is not available.
treatment: Remove the contaminated feed immediately — this is the only specific treatment
Provide clean feed and good-quality forage
Use a toxin binder in the feed — hydrated sodium calcium aluminosilicate or yeast cell wall products — to reduce absorption
Supportive care: fluids, liver support with antioxidants and methionine, and vitamin E supplementation
Do not feed contaminated milk or produce to humans or calves
outbreak: Withdraw the suspect feed and submit samples for analysis
Identify the contaminated batch and its source
Test milk for aflatoxin M1 if dairy cattle are involved, and withhold contaminated milk
Review storage and feed procurement practices
public_health: Aflatoxin is a Group 1 human carcinogen and a major cause of hepatocellular carcinoma in sub-Saharan Africa
Chronic dietary exposure causes childhood stunting and immune impairment
Aflatoxin M1 in milk is a regulated contaminant, and milk from exposed cows must not enter the human food chain
Maize and groundnuts for human consumption should be tested and stored properly; sorting and processing reduce contamination but do not eliminate it
control.notes: Aflatoxin is heat-stable — cooking, baking and normal feed processing do not destroy it. Prevention is entirely a matter of storage and sourcing.

prognosis: Good if exposure is removed early and liver damage is limited. Poor in acute high-dose outbreaks with severe hepatic necrosis, where mortality can be significant. Chronic exposure causes permanent production loss and, in dairy cattle, persistent milk residue risk.
